title: Optimize cost reduction roadmap + quantization library demo (Northstar Search)
topics: Northstar current inference architecture and traffic profile
Quantization Profile Library: what it is, how enablement works (route-level)
Quality guardrails and evals (A/B, thresholds, rollback triggers)
Observability: dashboards, audit logs, applied vs fallback signals
Security/compliance: RBAC, auditability, data retention, VPC/dedicated
summary: Redwood walked Northstar Search through the Optmize roadmap and a demo of the upcoming opt-in Quantization Profile Library. Northstar is cost-sensitive on reranking + generation routes and is considering moving more traffic from self-hosted vLLM and some Bedrock usage. They asked for: (1) per-route enablement with version pinning (no silent changes), (2) a clear GPU/model compatibility matrix (H100/A100/L4), (3) a way to run offline evals on their prompt sets before enabling, (4) audit logs + RBAC controls suitable for enterprise change control, and (5) rollback mechanisms including an emergency kill switch. Redwood aligned on a beta path: start with one rerank route and one chat route, run Redwood’s eval harness + perf suite, and then canary enable to 1–5% traffic with monitoring of quality + p95 latency and fallback rate.
action_items: Redwood (Markus) to send Northstar the beta one-pager and a short deck covering route-level enablement, profile versioning, and rollback controls.
Redwood (Arjun/Jonas) to share example profile schema fields + a sample compatibility matrix for H100/A100/L4 and max context constraints.
Northstar (Rina) to provide target models + approximate context length distribution and top 2 workloads (rerank vs chat) with current p50/p95 latency and token rates.
Northstar (Sam) to confirm current GPU mix and whether they need dedicated capacity or can use hosted for initial pilot.
Northstar (Lena) to send security questionnaire items specifically around audit logs, RBAC, and retention; Redwood to respond with controls and log field list.
next_steps: Schedule a 45-min technical follow-up focused on Northstar’s two candidate routes and model choices (next week).
Set up a pilot workspace with an allowlisted Console toggle for route-level quantization settings.
Run an offline A/B eval on Northstar’s prompt set (baseline vs proposed profile) before any production canary.
transcript:
Meeting: Optimize cost reduction roadmap + quantization library demo (Northstar Search)
Recorded: 2025-02-19 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 53 min

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood) 
- Arjun Desai (Redwood)
- Jonas Weber (Redwood)
- Paula Mendes (Redwood)
- Evan Cho (Northstar Search, CTO)
- Rina Kapoor (Northstar Search, ML Platform)
- Sam Ortega (Northstar Search, Infra/DevOps)
- Lena Wu (Northstar Search, Security)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Redwood presented Optimize roadmap and an early look at Quantization Profile Library (opt-in, route-level).
- Northstar asked about version pinning, compatibility matrix, quality gates, and audit/change controls.
- Agreed to scope a pilot on 1 rerank route + 1 chat route with offline eval + canary.


[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, alright, thanks everyone for making time. I know it’s a mixed group, which is great. Goal today is two parts: one, quick Optimize roadmap—what we’re doing this quarter on cost controls. Two, a demo slash walkthrough of our Quantization Profile Library concept. It’s opt-in, route-level. And then we’ll spend time on your requirements—models, latency, any compliance constraints.

[00:23] Evan Cho: Sounds good.

[00:25] Markus Klein: Rina, Sam, Lena—anything you want to make sure we hit?

[00:30] Rina Kapoor: For me, mainly, what models are supported and like, how you prevent quality regressions. We’ve been burned by “fast mode” type features before.

[00:39] Lena Wu: And for security, I’m looking for audit logs and change control. If someone flips a toggle, we need to know who, when, what changed.

[00:47] Sam Ortega: And operationally, what happens if it’s incompatible. Like, we have mixed GPU fleets.

[00:52] Markus Klein: Perfect. Arjun’s gonna go deeper on the profile library, Jonas will speak to evals and regression thresholds, and Paula can cover the dashboards and rollout telemetry.

[01:06] Paula Mendes: Hey everyone.

[01:08] Arjun Desai: Hi.

[01:10] Jonas Weber: Hey.


[01:14] Markus Klein: Quick context check first. Evan, can you give us the 60 seconds on Northstar’s inference stack today?

[01:22] Evan Cho: Sure. We’re search and recommendations. We do reranking with a smaller transformer, and we also have a chat-ish assistant in product. Right now, rerank is mostly self-hosted. We’re on vLLM. And the chat route is… mixed. Some on Bedrock for a model we can’t host, and some open models in our cluster.

[01:45] Markus Klein: Okay.

[01:46] Evan Cho: We’re trying to bring more under one roof and reduce GPU burn. The biggest pain is our peak hours. We either overprovision or we get tail latency spikes.

[01:58] Markus Klein: Got it. Rina, what models are you using for rerank + chat today?

[02:03] Rina Kapoor: Rerank is a fine-tuned encoder, kind of a BERT-y thing, but we’re testing a bigger cross-encoder too. For chat, we have a Llama 3 variant internally. Context lengths are usually not huge, like maybe 4k typical, but we do have some long tail to 16k.

[02:23] Jonas Weber: When you say tail to 16k, is that like 1% of requests or more?

[02:27] Rina Kapoor: Less than 1%. Maybe 0.3%. But it matters because those are high-value users.

[02:34] Markus Klein: And latency SLOs—what’s your p95 target for rerank and chat?

[02:40] Sam Ortega: Rerank is strict. We’re trying to keep p95 under 250 ms end-to-end. Model itself ideally 100-ish. Chat is looser, like p95 under 900 ms for first token, streaming after.

[02:56] Markus Klein: Great. That’s super helpful.


[03:00] Markus Klein: Okay, Optimize roadmap in 2 minutes. Our theme is “cost levers with guardrails.” So: better batching suggestions, KV/prefix cache tuning, and this quantization library where we publish per-model quant profiles that are tested, versioned, and then you can enable them per route. It’s not going to auto-enable. You choose.

[03:22] Evan Cho: So not like a global “make it cheaper” switch.

[03:24] Markus Klein: Exactly. V1 is route-level toggle, and you can scope by region or deployment tier depending on how you run.

[03:31] Paula Mendes: And the console will show you what percent of traffic is on a profile, plus fallback rate—like if it tried to apply and didn’t.

[03:39] Sam Ortega: I like the fallback metric. We’ve had silent “falls back to CPU” type behaviors in other places.

[03:45] Paula Mendes: Yeah, this would be explicit.


[03:49] Markus Klein: Arjun, want to take the main demo?

[03:52] Arjun Desai: Yep. So, Quantization Profile Library: think of it like a catalog entry attached to a model variant. Each profile is versioned. It defines things like quant method—INT8, FP8 mixed, weight-only, activation quant, etc—plus hardware constraints, max context it’s validated for, known caveats. Then, your route config references a profile ref. If you don’t set anything, behavior stays baseline.

[04:21] Rina Kapoor: When you say “profile ref,” is it like “latest” or an exact version?

[04:26] Arjun Desai: Good question. Default is explicit version pinning. Like `profile_id: llama3-70b-int8-v3`—I’m making up the name. We’re cautious about a “latest” alias because it could change behavior without your action.

[04:41] Evan Cho: Thank you.

[04:42] Arjun Desai: We may support an alias like “recommended” but it would require an explicit opt-in and we’d surface change history.

[04:52] Lena Wu: So if it changes, that’s an audit event?

[04:55] Arjun Desai: Yes. And if you pin to a version, it won’t change.


[05:01] Arjun Desai: The key design principle is deterministic selection. When the request comes in, the control plane resolves: route setting + tenant overrides + global kill switch. It returns either “apply profile X” or “disabled” or “fallback to baseline because incompatible.” The runtime gets a resolved decision and applies it.

[05:22] Sam Ortega: What does “incompatible” cover?

[05:25] Arjun Desai: Model mismatch, GPU class mismatch, unsupported context length range, sometimes batch size constraints. Also deployment tier constraints—like we might only validate a profile on H100 and not on, say, L4.

[05:40] Sam Ortega: We have H100 in one region and A100 in another.

[05:43] Arjun Desai: Then we’d likely either publish separate profiles or mark constraints. The policy engine would pick baseline if it doesn’t match.

[05:52] Sam Ortega: And it doesn’t crash the request.

[05:54] Arjun Desai: Correct, it should not. Fallback is part of the contract.


[06:00] Jonas Weber: Maybe I’ll add: we also monitor fallback rate. If it spikes, you’ll see it, and it can alert.

[06:06] Paula Mendes: Right, and you can break it down by route and region.


[06:12] Markus Klein: I’m going to share screen for a second just conceptually. (pause) So imagine in Console under Route Settings there’s a “Quantization” section. It shows “Off (default)” or “Enabled: Profile X.” When you click enable, it shows compatibility warnings: “This profile validated on H100, max context 8k, your route is configured max 16k.” That kind of thing.

[06:37] Rina Kapoor: Can it block you from enabling if it’s obviously wrong?

[06:41] Markus Klein: Yes, for hard incompatibilities it blocks. For soft risks, it warns and requires confirmation.

[06:48] Lena Wu: Is that configurable per tenant? Like we might want “only admins can override warnings.”

[06:54] Paula Mendes: RBAC is on the change action. So you can scope who can write route settings. We’ve seen customers do “read-only for most, write for platform admins.”

[07:05] Lena Wu: And do you support approvals? Like two-person review.

[07:08] Markus Klein: Not a full approval workflow in v1. But we do have audit logs and change history. Some customers pair it with their own change management process. We can talk about what’s required for your policy.


[07:22] Arjun Desai: One more thing: profiles are “published” only after internal validation. So the library itself is curated, not “upload your own random quant.” V1 is Redwood-provided profiles.

[07:34] Evan Cho: Are you planning to let customers bring their own later?

[07:36] Arjun Desai: Later, possibly. It’s out of scope for v1 because safety and support burden.


[07:44] Jonas Weber: On quality: we run a set of prompt sets and eval suites. We look at deltas by task family. If a profile has a statistically significant degradation beyond threshold, it doesn’t publish.

[07:57] Rina Kapoor: What metrics? BLEU? That stuff is not meaningful for us.

[08:02] Jonas Weber: Yeah, depends. For generation we use a mix: task-specific scoring, some rubric-based LLM-as-judge with controls, and also regression on known “golden” prompts. For embeddings/rerank it’s different—NDCG, MRR, pairwise accuracy, etc.

[08:18] Rina Kapoor: Okay. We care about ranking metrics for rerank.

[08:22] Jonas Weber: Exactly.


[08:25] Sam Ortega: How do you ensure latency doesn’t get worse? Sometimes quantization helps throughput but hurts tail.

[08:31] Jonas Weber: We benchmark p50/p95 decode, prefill time, and memory footprint. Some profiles can increase memory pressure, which can hurt tail. If we see that, we constrain the profile or don’t ship it.

[08:45] Paula Mendes: And in production you’d see latency deltas per route when enabled. There are panels for p95 + cost per 1k tokens or per request depending on endpoint.


[08:57] Evan Cho: Let me ask a practical one. If we enable on a route and there’s an issue, rollback is just turning it off?

[09:03] Markus Klein: Yes. Route-level disable is fastest. And there’s also a platform-level kill switch we can flip if something systemic happens.

[09:10] Lena Wu: Who can flip kill switch.

[09:12] Markus Klein: That’s Redwood internal SRE for emergency. For customers, you can disable at route level yourself. For Dedicated/Private we can discuss if you want an “admin kill switch” in your control plane; depends on deployment mode.

[09:26] Sam Ortega: We’d probably want that for dedicated.


[09:30] Markus Klein: Let’s get into your requirements. Rina—what are the first two routes you’d consider enabling a profile on?

[09:37] Rina Kapoor: Chat route is the biggest spend, but rerank is most sensitive to quality. So maybe start with chat because we can watch user feedback.

[09:47] Evan Cho: I’d say start with rerank but on a small canary. If it works there, it’s a huge win.

[09:55] Rina Kapoor: (laughs) We can argue offline. But okay, maybe one of each.

[10:01] Markus Klein: That’s actually a common approach. One “quality-sensitive” and one “cost-heavy.”


[10:07] Paula Mendes: For canary, what percent traffic can you safely route to an experiment?

[10:12] Sam Ortega: For rerank, we can do 1% initially. For chat, 5%.

[10:17] Paula Mendes: Great.


[10:19] Jonas Weber: And do you have a prompt set or offline dataset we can run evals against? Even like a sample of last week’s queries.

[10:27] Rina Kapoor: Yes, we can provide anonymized queries and relevance labels for rerank. For chat, we can provide some conversation snippets but we need to strip PII.

[10:38] Lena Wu: That’s key. We can’t send raw customer data to a third party without controls.

[10:43] Markus Klein: Understood. For hosted API we can sign DPA, and we have SOC 2. If you need VPC or Dedicated with data isolation, we can do that for a pilot depending on scope.

[10:57] Lena Wu: We will need at least SOC 2 report and details on retention.

[11:01] Markus Klein: Yep.


[11:03] Lena Wu: Also, where are audit logs stored and can we export to SIEM.

[11:08] Paula Mendes: Audit events are in the control plane and can be exported. Specifically for quant settings we log actor, route id, old value/new value, and the profile id applied. There’s also a request-time annotation—like `quant_profile_id`—in tracing.

[11:25] Sam Ortega: Wait, request-time annotation is in logs? Like we can query, “did this request use quant.”

[11:31] Paula Mendes: Yes. It’s tagged as “applied” vs “fallback” vs “disabled.”

[11:36] Sam Ortega: That’s huge.


[11:39] Arjun Desai: And determinism matters there—if you replay config at time T, the system should have applied the same decision. No random selection.

[11:48] Evan Cho: How do you avoid like, it fetches profile metadata and causes latency spikes.

[11:54] Arjun Desai: We cache the resolved profile metadata. We don’t fetch per request from the registry. Runtime loads artifacts out-of-band. Also rate limits and caching to prevent thundering herd.

[12:10] Sam Ortega: We had a thing where model cards were fetched too often and it DoS’d internal services. So yeah, I’m glad you mentioned it.


[12:20] Markus Klein: On models: you mentioned Llama 3 variant. Which sizes?

[12:24] Rina Kapoor: 8B and 70B, mostly. 70B is expensive.

[12:30] Arjun Desai: That’s a top candidate for profiles. We’ve seen meaningful cost per token reductions on 70B with mixed precision, but it depends on GPU.

[12:40] Rina Kapoor: What GPU.

[12:41] Arjun Desai: H100 is best. A100 can still benefit but constraints differ.

[12:47] Sam Ortega: We’re like 60% A100, 40% H100, plus some L4 for dev.

[12:53] Arjun Desai: L4 is tricky for some profiles; we’d likely have separate “safe” profiles or no profile. But we can formalize in a compatibility matrix.


[13:05] Jonas Weber: On context length: if you have a 16k tail, we might constrain a profile to 8k, so requests above that fall back automatically. The user experience remains correct, just not cheaper for that request.

[13:19] Evan Cho: That’s acceptable.

[13:20] Rina Kapoor: As long as it’s visible.

[13:22] Paula Mendes: It’ll show in fallback reason metrics.


[13:26] Lena Wu: I want to be very explicit: if it falls back, is it logged, and can we alert.

[13:31] Paula Mendes: Yes. Metric is like `quant_profile_fallback_rate` by route/model/region, with reason tags. We can set alert thresholds.

[13:41] Lena Wu: Good.


[13:43] Markus Klein: Any other compliance constraints? Data residency?

[13:47] Lena Wu: We have EU users, but for this pilot we can keep it US-only. Long term we need EU processing. Also, we need SSO. SAML ideally.

[13:58] Markus Klein: SSO is supported on the enterprise tier. For pilot, we can still set up RBAC. For EU, we have EU regions available; the feature should behave the same.


[14:10] Evan Cho: What about “private deployment.” We’re not ready for on-prem, but VPC maybe.

[14:15] Markus Klein: VPC / Private is an option. The quant library is the same schema; control plane resolution is the same; just deployed in your environment.

[14:24] Sam Ortega: That’s important, we don’t want a feature that only works in hosted.

[14:28] Markus Klein: Yep, consistency is core.


[14:33] Rina Kapoor: Can you talk about how profiles are created? Like calibration sets and all that.

[14:39] Arjun Desai: Sure. At a high level, we calibrate against a dataset (internal prompt sets, sometimes public corpora), then we validate with our eval harness. The profile metadata includes references to calibration dataset IDs, the quant method, and known caveats.

[14:55] Rina Kapoor: Do we get to see those dataset IDs?

[14:58] Arjun Desai: Yes, in the profile metadata. But not necessarily the data itself if it’s internal. We can also run a “customer eval pack” with your data to confirm.


[15:10] Jonas Weber: And that’s really the gate for your use case—your own evaluation on your prompt set.

[15:15] Rina Kapoor: Yep.


[15:17] Evan Cho: Let’s talk cost reduction. What are realistic savings?

[15:22] Arjun Desai: Depends. For some decode-heavy workloads, we’ve seen 15–30% cost per token improvement. But it’s not universal; sometimes it’s more about throughput or fitting in memory.

[15:35] Jonas Weber: And sometimes the “savings” are actually that you can batch better because of memory headroom.

[15:40] Sam Ortega: Right.


[15:42] Markus Klein: We’ll be careful not to over-promise; we’d benchmark on your workloads.


[16:00] (crosstalk)
[16:01] Rina Kapoor: Sorry, one more question—can we choose quant per region? Because our H100 region is west and A100 is east.

[16:08] Markus Klein: Yes, route-level with optional region constraints. Or you can have separate routes per region. The policy system can resolve with region in the context.

[16:19] Sam Ortega: Okay.


[16:22] Lena Wu: What about change windows? If someone changes a profile setting at noon, does it instantly apply.

[16:28] Paula Mendes: It applies after config propagation. Typically within a minute or so. We can also do scheduled changes, but that’s not in v1 for this feature specifically.

[16:38] Lena Wu: Then we need internal process to restrict who can do it.

[16:41] Markus Klein: Yep, RBAC.


[16:45] Jonas Weber: Maybe we should outline the rollout plan for you: offline eval first, then enable in a staging or perf-canary environment, then 1% in prod, watch quality and latency and fallback rate, then ramp.

[16:58] Evan Cho: That’s what we want.


[17:02] Markus Klein: Cool. Let’s dig into your candidate models and endpoints. Rina, for chat, is it standard chat completion endpoint with streaming?

[17:10] Rina Kapoor: Yes. We do function calling occasionally. Also structured JSON output for some flows.

[17:17] Arjun Desai: Quantization shouldn’t change the API surface. But quality could affect structured output adherence. We should include that in evals—like JSON validity rates.

[17:29] Rina Kapoor: Exactly.


[17:32] Jonas Weber: For rerank, are you doing embeddings + rerank or pure cross-encoder rerank.

[17:38] Rina Kapoor: Both. First pass is embeddings. Second pass is rerank for top 50.

[17:44] Jonas Weber: Great—profiles may differ between embedding model and rerank model.


[18:00] Sam Ortega: How does this interact with caching? We do a lot of prompt prefix caching.

[18:06] Arjun Desai: Good catch. KV cache formats can differ depending on precision path. The runtime handles it, but you can’t share KV caches across quant and non-quant modes unless it’s compatible. The safe approach is treat them as separate cache keys.

[18:20] Sam Ortega: Okay, so enabling could reduce cache hit rate.

[18:23] Arjun Desai: Potentially, if you mix modes on the same route. That’s why route-level is nice—you keep it consistent.

[18:31] Paula Mendes: And we can show cache hit rate deltas too, at least at a high level.


[18:40] Evan Cho: This is getting in the weeds, but good.


[18:44] Markus Klein: Competitor question—how are you evaluating alternatives? Just so we understand.

[18:49] Evan Cho: We talked to Together AI a bit. Also Anyscale. And obviously AWS is always there. But we want more control and better observability.

[19:02] Markus Klein: Makes sense.


[19:05] Lena Wu: And for AWS, audit logs and IAM are strong. So Redwood needs to match enough of that.

[19:11] Markus Klein: Understood. We won’t claim to be AWS, but we do have audit logging, RBAC, SSO, and export capabilities.


[19:20] Paula Mendes: Quick clarification—do you need retention policies for logs? Like 30/90 days.

[19:26] Lena Wu: 90 days minimum. For audit logs, longer. We export to SIEM.

[19:33] Paula Mendes: Okay.


[19:36] Jonas Weber: For eval gating, are you okay with Redwood’s thresholds, or do you want to set your own acceptance criteria.

[19:42] Rina Kapoor: We want our own. Like no more than, I don’t know, 0.2% drop on NDCG@10, and for chat we’ll do human review plus JSON validity.

[19:54] Jonas Weber: Great. We can set custom gates for your pilot.


[20:00] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about timeline. When would you want to start a pilot.

[20:06] Evan Cho: March. We’re planning a cost reduction push end of Q1.

[20:11] Sam Ortega: But if it’s behind a feature flag, we can start earlier in staging.

[20:15] Markus Klein: We can likely do that. This is in beta timeline. We can allowlist your workspace.


[20:25] (brief audio cut)
[20:27] Markus Klein: Sorry, I think I froze for a second. Can you all hear me.

[20:29] Rina Kapoor: Yep.


[20:31] Arjun Desai: On deliverables: we’ll share a sample schema and compatibility matrix. It’ll show GPU classes, max context validated, and whether it supports tool calling—well, tool calling is more “quality risk” than compatibility, but we can annotate.

[20:52] Rina Kapoor: That would be helpful.


[20:55] Lena Wu: Also please include which events are in audit logs. We need field-level details for compliance.

[21:01] Paula Mendes: Yep.


[21:05] Sam Ortega: Another operational question: if a profile is deprecated, what happens to pinned versions.

[21:11] Arjun Desai: Pinned versions continue to exist for a deprecation window. We’d mark it as deprecated and give you notice. Eventually we might remove it, but we’d coordinate. For “recommended” alias, we could move it, but again that would be an explicit opt-in.

[21:28] Sam Ortega: Okay.


[21:30] Evan Cho: I want to make sure we don’t end up in a situation where you fix a profile and suddenly we get different behavior without changing config.

[21:38] Markus Klein: That’s exactly why pinning is the default.


[21:42] Jonas Weber: Also, if we detect a quality regression, we can block publication or disable availability for certain model variants. But that doesn’t force-change your route. It just prevents new enablement, unless it’s critical safety in which case we’d coordinate.

[21:58] Evan Cho: Okay.


[22:00] Rina Kapoor: Can you talk about how you label “experimental.”

[22:04] Arjun Desai: Yes. Profiles can have a maturity field. Experimental means limited validation set, maybe only internal benchmarks. Stable means it passed full eval suite and perf suite.

[22:16] Rina Kapoor: We’d only use stable.

[22:18] Arjun Desai: Totally fair.


[22:20] Markus Klein: We’re about halfway. Maybe we shift to concrete scoping. Rina, can you list the top two models you want us to cover.

[22:28] Rina Kapoor: Llama 3 70B for chat. And for rerank, we’re deciding between a cross-encoder around 1–3B and a smaller one. I can send exact model ids.

[22:40] Markus Klein: Great.


[22:42] Sam Ortega: And endpoints: chat completion, embeddings, rerank. We use streaming in chat.

[22:48] Markus Klein: Cool.


[22:50] Lena Wu: Deployment mode: if we start hosted, do you store prompts.

[22:55] Markus Klein: By default we don’t use prompts for training. Logging/retention is configurable; we can minimize what’s stored. For some enterprise settings we can do zero retention beyond operational metrics. We’ll put it in writing.

[23:12] Lena Wu: Okay.


[23:14] Jonas Weber: From an eval standpoint, we’d prefer you provide sanitized prompt sets. Or we can run eval in your environment if that’s required.

[23:22] Sam Ortega: For rerank we can provide sanitized. For chat, we might need to run internally.

[23:28] Markus Klein: We can discuss private pilot options.


[23:35] Paula Mendes: Telemetry requirements: do you want cost attribution by team or route.

[23:40] Evan Cho: Route is enough.

[23:42] Rina Kapoor: We want per route and per model variant, plus region.

[23:48] Paula Mendes: Great.


[24:00] Markus Klein: Any other objections or concerns.

[24:04] Rina Kapoor: Just the usual—quantization is scary. I want the ability to A/B quickly and roll back quickly.

[24:12] Markus Klein: Yes.

[24:13] Jonas Weber: Our playbook is basically: offline eval -> staging -> 1% canary -> ramp. And we define rollback triggers up front.

[24:22] Rina Kapoor: Good.


[24:24] Lena Wu: And that rollback action is audited.

[24:26] Paula Mendes: Yep.


[24:28] Sam Ortega: If you have a profile only compatible on H100, and traffic shifts to A100 due to capacity, do you get mixed behavior within a route.

[24:37] Arjun Desai: Potentially yes, but it will be baseline on A100 and quant on H100. That’s why we log applied vs fallback and we recommend scoping routes by hardware pool if you want consistency.

[24:52] Sam Ortega: Okay. We might do separate routes.

[24:55] Markus Klein: Yep.


[25:00] Evan Cho: Can I ask about pricing. Is this included or add-on.

[25:04] Markus Klein: For beta, we’re not charging extra for the feature itself. Longer term, it’ll likely be part of Optimize package, but details are still being finalized. The cost savings are the main benefit.

[25:16] Evan Cho: Okay.


[25:20] (pause)

[25:22] Markus Klein: We’ve got about 10 minutes left. Let’s do a recap + next steps, unless there’s a final technical rabbit hole.

[25:29] Rina Kapoor: Maybe one last: structured output. If quant reduces JSON validity, will you catch it.

[25:35] Jonas Weber: We can add that as a metric in eval. Also in production, you can track parsing failure rate on your side. We can add a dashboard panel if you emit that metric.

[25:46] Rina Kapoor: Okay.


[25:48] Lena Wu: For audit exports, can you provide a sample event.

[25:52] Paula Mendes: Yes, we’ll send a redacted sample. It includes route id, actor, timestamp, old/new profile id, and a correlation id.

[26:02] Lena Wu: Perfect.


[26:05] Markus Klein: Recap: we’ll send beta one-pager + deck, Arjun and Jonas will share schema example + initial compatibility matrix, Paula will share audit log fields and telemetry panels. On your side, Rina will send the candidate model ids and your context length distribution, Sam will confirm GPU mix and whether hosted vs dedicated for pilot, Lena will send security questionnaire.

[26:31] Evan Cho: Sounds right.

[26:33] Markus Klein: And then we schedule a technical follow-up next week to pick the two routes and define success metrics and rollback triggers.

[26:41] Sam Ortega: Works.

[26:42] Rina Kapoor: Yep.

[26:44] Lena Wu: Okay.


[26:46] Markus Klein: Awesome. Thanks everyone.

[26:49] (meeting ends)

Note: Transcript may be truncated in places due to overlapping speech and minor audio drops.
